title: Pending EMI requests
objective: EMI requests are sitting in a pending state and never completing. Move them to completion.
reviewerNotes: Unlike S1 the customer HAS acted, so the EMI request lifecycle is the right entry here. The contrast with S1 is the point: the same subject, a different point in the sequence.
watchFor: entry on the transaction when the request already exists

questions: Should messaging differ by EMI Product Type or Source (e.g. a Txn-to-EMI conversion vs an Onboarding-originated request), since the 'last step' a customer needs to do may differ?

strategy.summary: EMI requests enter a 'Pending' state and often stall before completion. The campaign enters the moment a request becomes Pending (the opportunity point) and nudges the customer, via increasingly higher-touch channels, to finish it before the request auto-expires at day 7. The goal is the request's own status flipping to Successful, checked automatically after every step so converted customers stop receiving messages immediately.
approach: Entry on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED / New Status = Pending — this is the exact moment the opportunity exists and hasn't yet resolved, which is the only entity/event that represents 'an open EMI request'.
Goal on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED / New Status = Successful — the only event that proves the behaviour (completion), on the same entity so it's a valid comparison.

Three sends spaced 48h apart (0h/48h/96h), channel order EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP: lead with the cheapest channel per preference, reserve WhatsApp as a higher-touch recovery attempt closer to the 7-day expiry (P-010 hypothesis, P-009/P-011 constraints respected).

Deliberately used only 3 of the 4 allowed messages, finishing by hour 96 — leaves buffer before the day-7 Expired cutoff (P-003) and favours the stated conservative preference for fewer, better-targeted messages over maxing out the cap.

10% control group applied per stated preference, so any later read of this journey's effect (even informally) isn't confounded with 'what would have happened anyway' (P-006) — though no lift claim is made here given no historical data exists.

rejected.why: Would only catch a snapshot of existing pending requests, not continuously catch newly-created ones, and risks re-entering the same customer repeatedly outside the event-driven model.

rejected.option: Branching mid-journey on Failed/Expired/Cancelled via a condition step
rejected.why: The condition/SPLIT step type only reads a previous SEND's delivery outcome (e.g. DELIVERED/FAILED), not a business event like EMI status — there is no supported way to fork the journey on Failed/Cancelled mid-flight. Flagged as an operational limitation below rather than invented around.

rejected.option: Using all 4 allowed messages / tighter 24-36h spacing
rejected.why: Would reduce buffer before the 7-day expiry and increase fatigue risk; conservative risk appetite and P-011 favour fewer, well-spaced messages.

P-005 says change one variable at a time, and there's no baseline to compare against yet. One coherent hypothesis-driven sequence is the simpler, defensible first iteration; an experiment can follow once there's a baseline.

assumptions: No segmentation by EMI Product Type (Single-Txn/Multi-Txn/Outstanding) or Source — one generic message set applies to all pending requests. Default chosen for simplicity; flagged below.

EMI_STATUS_CHANGED (EMI Request entity) is marked 'new-proposed' in platform metadata — i.e. not confirmed built in production. The whole entry/goal/branch design above depends on this event actually firing; this is a stated limitation, not a verified capability.
DNC and NPA exclusion are applied as hard constraints per tenant policy; quiet hours (21:00–09:00) govern actual send timing even though step waits are specified in hours.
evidenceNotes: No historical data exists on why pending EMI requests stall (OTP drop-off, document step, manual review, etc.). That data would sharpen message content (e.g. naming the specific blocking step) but isn't a prerequisite — proceeding with a generic 'finish the last step' message and noting this as a gap.

steps.name: Initial completion nudge
steps.copy: Hi ${customerFirstName}, your EMI request just needs one more step to go through. Finish it now so your purchase can be converted to easy instalments.

steps.name: Mid-window reminder
steps.copy: Reminder: your EMI request is still pending and only stays open for a limited time. Complete the last step today.

steps.name: Final reminder before expiry
steps.copy: Last reminder: your EMI request closes soon if it isn't completed. Finish it today to keep your instalment plan.

turns.reply:
EMI requests enter a 'Pending' state and often stall before completion. The campaign enters the moment a request becomes Pending (the opportunity point) and nudges the customer, via increasingly higher-touch channels, to finish it before the request auto-expires at day 7. The goal is the request's own status flipping to Successful, checked automatically after every step so converted customers stop receiving messages immediately.

**Approach**
- Entry on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED / New Status = Pending — this is the exact moment the opportunity exists and hasn't yet resolved, which is the only entity/event that represents 'an open EMI request'.
- Goal on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED / New Status = Successful — the only event that proves the behaviour (completion), on the same entity so it's a valid comparison.
- Three sends spaced 48h apart (0h/48h/96h), channel order EMAIL → SMS → WHATSAPP: lead with the cheapest channel per preference, reserve WhatsApp as a higher-touch recovery attempt closer to the 7-day expiry (P-010 hypothesis, P-009/P-011 constraints respected).
- Deliberately used only 3 of the 4 allowed messages, finishing by hour 96 — leaves buffer before the day-7 Expired cutoff (P-003) and favours the stated conservative preference for fewer, better-targeted messages over maxing out the cap.
- 10% control group applied per stated preference, so any later read of this journey's effect (even informally) isn't confounded with 'what would have happened anyway' (P-006) — though no lift claim is made here given no historical data exists.

**Considered and not used**
- Audience (segment) entry on currently-pending requests — Would only catch a snapshot of existing pending requests, not continuously catch newly-created ones, and risks re-entering the same customer repeatedly outside the event-driven model.
- Branching mid-journey on Failed/Expired/Cancelled via a condition step — The condition/SPLIT step type only reads a previous SEND's delivery outcome (e.g. DELIVERED/FAILED), not a business event like EMI status — there is no supported way to fork the journey on Failed/Cancelled mid-flight. Flagged as an operational limitation below rather than invented around.
- Using all 4 allowed messages / tighter 24-36h spacing — Would reduce buffer before the 7-day expiry and increase fatigue risk; conservative risk appetite and P-011 favour fewer, well-spaced messages.
- A/B testing channel order now — P-005 says change one variable at a time, and there's no baseline to compare against yet. One coherent hypothesis-driven sequence is the simpler, defensible first iteration; an experiment can follow once there's a baseline.

**Assumptions**
- No segmentation by EMI Product Type (Single-Txn/Multi-Txn/Outstanding) or Source — one generic message set applies to all pending requests. Default chosen for simplicity; flagged below.
- EMI_STATUS_CHANGED (EMI Request entity) is marked 'new-proposed' in platform metadata — i.e. not confirmed built in production. The whole entry/goal/branch design above depends on this event actually firing; this is a stated limitation, not a verified capability.
- DNC and NPA exclusion are applied as hard constraints per tenant policy; quiet hours (21:00–09:00) govern actual send timing even though step waits are specified in hours.

**Worth settling before this is built**
- Should messaging differ by EMI Product Type or Source (e.g. a Txn-to-EMI conversion vs an Onboarding-originated request), since the 'last step' a customer needs to do may differ? Would change the entry conditions (splitting into multiple entry variants) and the copy for each variant, likely improving relevance. Until then: Launch with one generic message set covering all EMI Request sources/product types.

**Data that would improve this**
- What does the drop-off funnel look like by day within the 7-day pending window (e.g. most expirations happen on day 2 vs day 6)? Would let reminder timing cluster around the actual drop-off point rather than even 48h spacing.

**Limitations**
- EMI Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
- The platform cannot branch this journey mid-flight on the EMI request later turning Failed/Cancelled (only a prior SEND's delivery outcome is branchable). Is it acceptable that a customer whose request fails or is cancelled still receives the remaining scheduled reminders (generic copy, not claiming the request is still open)? Determines whether we accept some wasted/slightly-mistimed sends to Failed/Cancelled customers, or whether a separate exclusion mechanism needs to be built outside this journey.
